<document>
# Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

*Review of Work and Employment Research. S. Achterberg, N. Iwu, F. Castell and J. Moreno. Review protocol registered before search.*

## Abstract

We systematically reviewed studies of reductions in scheduled working time of at least 10% with pay maintained, reporting a quantitative measure of output. Twenty-three studies (1998–2025; about 41,000 workers) met inclusion criteria. Pooled across studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0), with very high heterogeneity (I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4). Study design, the hours measure and the type of work explain much of the heterogeneity: controlled studies found smaller effects (+8.2%) than uncontrolled before–after studies (+18.7%), studies using actual hours found smaller effects (+7.9%) than those using scheduled hours (+16.6%), and per-worker output fell substantially in coverage-bound work (−8.9%) but not in discretionary work (+0.6%). There is evidence of small-study bias; adjusting for it reduces the pooled per-hour estimate to +9.1%. Effects show no sign of decay over time.

## Methods

**Search and inclusion.** We searched four bibliographic databases and two working-paper repositories, and contacted authors of known pilots. Studies were included if they (a) evaluated a reduction in scheduled hours of at least 10% with no reduction in pay; (b) reported output per worker or output per hour, or data from which either could be derived; and (c) had at least 50 workers. We excluded studies reporting only self-rated productivity. Of 412 records screened, 23 studies met the criteria.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome is the change in output per hour, expressed as a log ratio and converted back to a percentage for reporting. Where a study reported both scheduled and actual hours, we used actual hours. The secondary outcome is the change in output per worker. For controlled studies we used the difference relative to the comparison group; for uncontrolled studies, the change from baseline.

**Coding of work type.** Two coders independently classified each study's setting as *discretionary* (output can be produced at any time within a deadline: case processing, professional services, software, back-office work), *coverage-bound* (output depends on staff being present while demand arrives: counters, contact centres, retail floors, care rotas), or *mixed/unclear*. Agreement was high (κ = 0.84); disagreements were resolved by discussion.

**Synthesis.** Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation; moderators examined by meta-regression. Small-study effects assessed by funnel plot, Egger's regression test, and trim-and-fill.

## Included studies

Of the 23 studies, 9 had a comparison group (3 randomised, including the Varden County trial; 6 matched or difference-in-differences) and 14 were uncontrolled before–after designs, including the Halden multi-organisation pilot. Eight studies measured actual hours; 15 used scheduled hours only. Thirteen settings were coded discretionary, 7 coverage-bound and 3 mixed or unclear. Only two studies were in manufacturing, both in the mixed category. Follow-up ranged from 3 to 30 months (median 6). Output measures were record-based in 12 studies and manager-reported in 11.

## Results

### Pooled effects

Across all 23 studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0; I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4; I² = 74%). The prediction interval for output per hour runs from −4% to +34%, meaning that a new study in an unknown setting could plausibly find anything from a small loss to a very large gain.

### Moderators

**Table 1. Subgroup estimates of the change in output per hour and output per worker**

| Subgroup | k | Output per hour | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| **All studies** | 23 | +13.4% (8.1 to 19.0) | −1.8% (−4.9 to +1.4) |
| Controlled designs | 9 | +8.2% (4.0 to 12.6) | −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5) |
| Uncontrolled before–after | 14 | +18.7% (11.2 to 26.7) | −0.2% (−4.0 to +3.8) |
| Actual hours measured | 8 | +7.9% (3.6 to 12.4) | −3.9% (−7.8 to +0.1) |
| Scheduled hours only | 15 | +16.6% (9.9 to 23.7) | −0.6% (−4.3 to +3.3) |
| Record-based output | 12 | +9.7% (5.0 to 14.6) | −3.6% (−7.2 to +0.2) |
| Manager-reported output | 11 | +17.8% (10.0 to 26.1) | +0.4% (−3.9 to +4.9) |
| Discretionary work | 13 | +15.1% (8.8 to 21.8) | +0.6% (−2.8 to +4.1) |
| Coverage-bound work | 7 | +6.2% (1.1 to 11.6) | −8.9% (−13.1 to −4.5) |
| Mixed or unclear | 3 | +12.0% (−1.5 to 27.4) | −2.9% (−10.6 to +5.4) |

In a multiple meta-regression including design, hours measure and work type together, all three moderators remained associated with the effect, and together they explained 58% of between-study variance. The design and measurement moderators overlap heavily: 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, and 9 of the 14 used manager-reported output. Our data cannot fully separate them.

The work-type moderator is the clearest for the per-worker outcome. In discretionary work, output per worker was essentially unchanged in pooled estimates; in coverage-bound work, it fell by about 9%, consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%). The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work was real but too small to compensate for the hours lost.

Note that the discretionary estimate of +15.1% per hour mixes controlled and uncontrolled studies. Restricting to the five controlled discretionary studies, the per-hour estimate is +9.6% (4.8 to 14.6) and the per-worker estimate −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2).

### Small-study effects

The funnel plot is asymmetric, with small studies reporting larger per-hour gains (Egger's test p = 0.02). Trim-and-fill imputes five missing studies on the left of the funnel and reduces the pooled per-hour estimate from +13.4% to +9.1% (95% CI 3.9 to 14.6). We interpret this as evidence that small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published or publicised than small, unfavourable ones.

### Duration

Four studies reported follow-up beyond 12 months. Their pooled per-hour gain was +14.0% (95% CI 6.2 to 22.4), indistinguishable from the overall estimate. Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside.

### Mechanisms

Eleven studies measured fatigue or wellbeing alongside output. Across these, the study-level correlation between the improvement in fatigue scores and the per-hour gain was weak (r = 0.18). Only three studies measured time spent in meetings, and none tested meetings as a mediator under a registered plan; we cannot assess this mechanism. Sick leave fell in all 14 studies that reported it (pooled −31%), and staff turnover fell in all 9 that reported it.

## Discussion

The literature supports a gain in output per hour from reduced working time, but a considerably smaller one than headline pilots suggest. The figure most often quoted, a gain of more than 20%, comes from uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours and manager-reported output; each of those features is associated with larger estimates. Controlled studies, studies measuring actual hours, studies using records, and the bias-adjusted estimate converge on a gain of roughly 8 to 10%.

Whether that gain is "enough" depends on the type of work. In discretionary settings the evidence is compatible with output per worker being maintained or falling slightly; in coverage-bound settings it falls clearly, and maintaining service would require additional staff.

We do not find support for the claim, made in one re-analysis of the Halden pilot, that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact. The controlled and actual-hours subgroups, which avoid the problems that re-analysis identified, still show gains whose confidence intervals exclude zero. Nor do we find support for the claim that reduced hours are sector-general.

## Limitations

Twenty-three studies is a small base for a meta-regression with three correlated moderators. Most studies are short. Only nine are controlled, and the controlled studies are themselves mostly in the public sector. Manufacturing and shift-based production are almost absent. Classification of work type, though reliable between coders, imposes a binary on what is often a mix within a single organisation.

</document>
response:
## Overall assessment

This is the most balanced of the four documents. It pre-registers its protocol, codes the obvious moderators, separates output per hour from output per worker, and reaches a middle-ground conclusion: a real but modest gain per hour of roughly 8–10%, and a clear loss of output per worker in work that depends on staff being present. That conclusion fits the Varden trial and both critiques of the Halden pilot.

The review has its own weak points. Its dismissal of the novelty explanation is as overstated as the Varga & Holm comment's "entirely an artifact" claim. Its correction for publication bias rests on a method that doesn't work well with this much variation between studies. And it presents several overlapping cuts of the same studies as if they were independent confirmations.

## Arithmetic and internal consistency (passes)

- **Study counts.** Every breakdown sums to 23: 9 controlled + 14 uncontrolled, 8 actual-hours + 15 scheduled-only, 13 discretionary + 7 coverage-bound + 3 mixed, and 12 record-based + 11 manager-reported.
- **Confidence intervals.** These are symmetric on the log scale, as they should be. For the pooled +13.4%, the interval runs ±0.048 around ln(1.134). The trim-and-fill interval is similarly symmetric.
- **Prediction interval.** The −4% to +34% range is centred correctly and implies between-study SD τ ≈ 0.076, which fits I² = 81%.
- **Per-hour versus per-worker.** For each subgroup, the two estimates together imply an hours reduction of about 11–16%. That is plausible for studies cutting hours by 10–25%.
- **Moderator overlap.** "12 of 14 uncontrolled used scheduled hours" leaves 6 of the 8 actual-hours studies among the controlled designs. So controlled designs and actual-hours measurement are almost the same group of studies, as the authors acknowledge.

## Main issues

**1. The duration section claims more than it shows.**
"Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside" rests on four studies, compared *between* studies rather than followed over time within each. There are several problems:
- **Confounding.** At +14.0%, the long-follow-up estimate is *higher* than the controlled-study estimate (+8.2%). That suggests the long studies are mostly uncontrolled or use scheduled hours, so their design inflates the estimate whatever happens over time. Duration should be entered into the meta-regression alongside design.
- **Survivorship.** Studies run past 12 months mostly in organisations that kept the scheme. Organisations that reverted, such as half of Halden's retail organisations, drop out of long-run evidence.
- **Wrong test.** Decay should be tested *within* studies, from each study's own month-by-month output data where reported.
- **Imprecision.** A confidence interval of 6.2% to 22.4% cannot rule out substantial decay.

A defensible statement would be that the limited long-run evidence does not show decay, but is too sparse and too confounded to rule it out. This mirrors the Varga & Holm comment, which treated a two-point survey trend as proof of novelty. Neither side's evidence on duration supports a firm conclusion.

**2. The publication-bias adjustment is unreliable here.**
- **Method limits.** Trim-and-fill is known to perform poorly when heterogeneity is high (I² = 81%).
- **Alternative explanation for the asymmetry.** The funnel asymmetry may come from the moderators the review has already identified: small studies are likely the uncontrolled pilots using scheduled hours and manager ratings. Interpreting it as selective publication is therefore not justified. The review should run Egger's test, or a precision-effect regression (PET-PEESE), *within* the moderator model to see whether the asymmetry survives.
- **Grey literature.** The search included contacting pilot authors, so some unpublished work was retrieved. That makes a publication-bias explanation less straightforward.

**3. The "convergence" is partly the same evidence counted several times.**
The Discussion says controlled studies, actual-hours studies, record-based studies and the bias-adjusted estimate "converge on roughly 8 to 10%". These groups overlap heavily: most controlled studies measure actual hours, and most likely use records. The trim-and-fill estimate also partly reflects the same design effects. This is one finding, that better-designed studies show smaller gains, not four independent ones. The cleaner approach is to report a single estimate from the best-designed studies, for example controlled designs with actual hours and record-based output. It would also help to report the three RCTs separately, even if that estimate is imprecise.

**4. Unclear handling of the Varden and Halden studies.**
- **Varden.** The trial reports two strata separately: case-processing at +12.5% per hour and counters at +6.7%. Because the work-type totals sum to 23, Varden must be entered as a single study. If it was coded "mixed", the review discards the only randomised comparison of the two work types. If it was split, the totals are wrong and the two entries are not independent. The authors should say which they did. Studies with stratum-level results should probably be split, with the dependence handled using robust variance estimation.
- **Halden.** The pilot spans six sectors, including retail. Which work type was it coded as? Was the original +23.4% used (scheduled hours, manager ratings), or the Varga & Holm corrected figures (actual hours, records, for subsets)? The rule "where a study reported both, we used actual hours" doesn't settle this, because the corrected figures come from a different publication.

**5. No formal risk-of-bias assessment.**
The review codes study design but doesn't apply a standard risk-of-bias tool (such as ROBINS-I or RoB 2) or grade the overall certainty of evidence (as GRADE does). Attrition is the clearest omission. Varga & Holm showed that nine Halden organisations dropped out *after* the schedule started, mostly citing workload. Organisations dropping out after the change has begun is likely in other voluntary pilots too, and nothing in the review captures it.

**6. The work-type finding should be separated from design.**
For discretionary work, the review gives a controlled-only estimate (+9.6% per hour, −2.7% per worker), which is good practice. It should do the same for coverage-bound work. If the seven coverage-bound studies are mostly controlled public-sector studies, the work-type contrast is partly a design contrast. The multiple meta-regression addresses this in principle, but the review doesn't report coefficients, and 23 studies with three correlated moderators is thin, as the authors acknowledge.

## Smaller points

- **Sick leave.** The pooled −31% is partly mechanical, as with Halden: fewer working days leave fewer days on which to be absent. The review should say whether studies counted sick *days* or sick *hours*. "Fell in all 14 studies" is vote-counting and should be replaced by a pooled estimate with an interval split by design.
- **The fatigue correlation (r = 0.18, 11 studies)** compares studies rather than individuals. It doesn't test fatigue as a mechanism, but it is mildly informative: it weakens Halden's claim that reduced fatigue is the "most plausible single explanation". The Discussion could say so.
- **Missing output-measure moderator.** Output measure (records versus manager ratings) is in Table 1 but left out of the multiple meta-regression, presumably because it is collinear with design. The review should say so explicitly.
- **Rebuttal of Varga & Holm.** The review says the controlled and actual-hours studies "avoid the problems that re-analysis identified". They avoid the denominator problem and some of the selection problem. They don't avoid attrition, unlogged working time (timesheets record claimed hours only), or a novelty boost in the group trying something new. "Not entirely an artifact" is supported. "Avoids those problems" is too strong.
- **Classification wording.** The limitations section calls the work-type coding "a binary", but it has three categories, including mixed/unclear.
- **Reporting.** There is no PRISMA flow diagram, and the dates of the 1998–2025 search aren't given.

## How the four documents fit together

| Document | Claimed per-hour gain | My assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Halden pilot | +23.4%, "sector-general" | Overstated: scheduled hours, manager ratings, survivors |
| Varden RCT | +12.5% case-processing, +6.7% counter | Most credible single study; few offices |
| Varga & Holm comment | 10.8% after corrections, then "entirely an artifact" | Good corrections, overreaching conclusion |
| This meta-analysis | ~8–10% in better studies | Sound central estimate; overreaches on novelty and bias correction |

The three later documents agree on the points that look secure:

- **Scheduled hours inflate the gain.** Per-hour gains computed against scheduled hours roughly double the real effect.
- **The best-designed evidence shows a modest real gain.** Controlled studies that measure actual hours put it at about 8–12% per hour.
- **Presence-bound work loses output.** Where output depends on staff being present, output per worker falls by about 9–11%, and maintaining service needs extra staff.

What remains open is whether the gains last beyond about a year, and how much of them comes from removing low-value time such as meetings rather than from rest. The meta-analysis is right that it cannot answer the second question. It should say the same about the first.

I can draft a reviewer report or a short synthesis note across all four documents if useful.
